.• ..,,.. , Th. neeklsdify she proceeded to lirunewiek,square, es usual; but Mtn. Ryan, having deeided to Nicol ( the day with her children at Sydenham, and not oaring to bear the expenses. of the governess, patron singly granted her a hololay. It,y walked homeward with fleet steps, ing 1 her unwonted freedom. She hatred at a book hop in Oxfordatreet, and requested to be alto od to look over an army-list. The request seas granted, and she turned over the book leave. w t a trembling hand. The name of Gray was fr and to I. not uneommon, hut there was Ili, colonel Gray belonging to an Indian regtmont who , old poasibly have belonged to euch a reginient ( seventeen yrare before. "I should have one of the old army lisle of the date in queatton," she thought. "He may be dead now. His regiment may be no longer in bolts. In view of the performance by the Warrington Musical .ociety on Wednesday next of Mendel- seohn's " nb,' we reproduce an article from .easselTs Magezi.," by Mr. John Crowily, a well- known writer on musical subjects, rim article, while foil of intrinsic interest as an analytical review of the mantel-piece of one of the greatest of our tone poets, If also be found an instructive preliminary to the forthcoming public performance of the work, which promises to be one of the coon- pletest which has been given in the interest of the Musical Society. The central figuis in " Elijah " newel his dominance' at the very commencement of the work. In contradio• 00,0 10 tlse usual course, he appears c--tire the overture, and in • declamatory plumage pronmincen the fateful prophecy which is to be loiflied in the occurrence of a , great and destructive drought. The overture, which immediately Nimes, depicts saltation and distre... in- crewing rspidly till the acme of intensity in reached In the rushing numbers of the closing bare, which prepare the mind fir the entry of the chorus, Help, Lord After the first appeal for help given lea few thrilling philter, the tenors introduce the (ipluisit..ly plaintive melody, "The beeves, now 'lancer. the summer days are gone," which is taken up by the other voicei.This forms material i-c the nest page or two of the chorus, and then is introduced the whispering passage "Will then the Lord be no more j 5d in bon." Here the voices for • time in•sve together, won, however, separating by recur. I thou', "is. by one to the subject just quoted, " The harvest now 1. over, the summer days are gone, and yet I no power rometh to help us The cries of" Help, 5 Lord !'' return in the mid* of this, but only in two of the parts, 311 • slight ecliJs, and prr s Idly the chorus of ~,misint grows less intense, Riving way at last to • group of descriptive passage' of choral recitation for the werai part, in turn, enumerating the distressing itsel- f/vets drought. In the neat number, Lord, bow Thine ear to out prs' !" i,m,minnrs the writer, • duet of soprano voices ie a comp...al, with anleinn, religious. and noteworthy effect, by the chorus, singing wally • sleek repenting pbraw of cccleeiwtical character—ll Lord, bow Thine j- our prayer I"—an Idea worthy of this ereat And of Which the beauty is appreciable hy every Ilstenet. • Mein, in time Arst choral number., brought the I 131:0frelniiVhnthcu'rrtIr d'etuel. the titre:7l'i; ironical effect. by introducing the prophet "Obadiah," who in a recitative point. out to Idolatrous Israel the path of rept•ntance, passing on to the well-known and truly lovely aria. "It with all your hear's ye truly scsk I me.'
